briefs.competency: classify geological faults according to the angle of the fault plane and direction of slip
briefs.content_standard: System models | Earthquakes | The Sun's influence on Earth
existing_facts_en:
Is an active fault the same as a plate edge?

Not exactly! An active fault is just a moving crack in the ground, while a plate boundary is the giant edge of huge earth slabs — a fault can even sit inside a plate.
As rocks on both sides of a fault slowly grind, stress builds up until it suddenly releases. That sudden slip causes an earthquake!

What causes an earthquake underground?

A fault is a crack in large underground rocks! When these two sides suddenly slip, an earthquake happens.

How do different faults move?

There are three main types! Normal faults pull apart, reverse faults push together, and strike-slip faults slide sideways past each other.
The Philippine Fault is a 'strike-slip' fault! Two huge blocks of land slide sideways past each other, like rubbing hands. When they suddenly slip, an earthquake happens!
If you stand on the Philippine Fault, the other side moves toward your left! This is called a 'left-lateral' fault, and it has been sliding this way for millions of years.
Not all mountain ranges come from folded land! Some form when a fault splits the crust—one block lifts up while the other drops. These fault-block mountains have steep, sharp sides.

How does the Philippine Fault Zone move?

This 1,200 km long strike-slip fault crosses the Philippines! It moves horizontally in a left-lateral sense: if you stand on it and look across, the far side moves left!
The Philippine Fault is a left-lateral strike-slip fault! This means its two sides slide sideways past each other.
The Marikina Valley Fault System in Luzon is a right-lateral strike-slip fault!

briefs.competency: explain why humans are classified under Class Mammalia and the Order Primates
briefs.content_standard: Organ systems working together | Heredity | Taxonomic classification | Photosynthesis, respiration and cycles in nature
existing_facts_en:
What animal is closest kin to us?

DNA studies show the colugo is the closest living relative of primates — that includes humans, monkeys, and tarsiers!

Is the tarsier really a monkey?

Many think the tarsier is a monkey, but it's not! It's a primate like monkeys and humans, but belongs to its own group and looks very different.

What is the scientific name of humans?

The scientific name of humans is Homo sapiens — Homo is the genus, and sapiens is the species.

What is the scientific name for humans?

It's Homo sapiens, Latin for 'wise man' — and every single person on Earth belongs to this one species!
Scientists have found that colugos are among the closest living relatives of primates like monkeys and humans.

Is the flying lemur really a lemur?

Nope! Its closest animal relatives are actually primates—the group with monkeys and humans—making it like our distant cousin!

What class do humans belong to?

Humans belong to the class Mammalia — that makes you a mammal too, just like dogs, cats, and whales!
The tarsier is not a monkey at all — it's a primate, a distant relative of both humans and monkeys.

What animal is a close cousin of monkeys?

The colugo! Scientists say it's one of the closest living relatives of primates like monkeys and humans.

Are humans the only ones with fingerprints?

No! Monkeys, gorillas, and even koalas have friction ridges on their fingers too, which help them grip. A koala's prints look surprisingly like a human's!

How many kinds of bats are there?

There are over a thousand kinds of bats in the world, one of the largest mammal groups around.

briefs.competency: identify what proportion of the Earth's surface is covered with water as opposed to land
briefs.content_standard: Distribution of the continents | Crustal features and interactions | Typhoons | Tides
existing_facts_en:
Is most of Earth's water safe for us to drink?

Nope! Most of Earth's water is in the oceans and is salty. Only a small part is fresh water we can drink.
About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water! That's exactly why our planet looks blue from space.

What exactly is sea level?

It's the average height of the ocean's surface, used as a measuring point for everything!
The ocean is super deep! At the Mariana Trench, it goes almost 11 kilometers down—deeper than the tallest mountain is tall!

Why is Earth called the "blue planet"?

Because oceans cover more than half of it! About 7 out of 10 parts of Earth's surface are water.

How many oceans are there on Earth?

There are five: Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Arctic, and Southern! The Pacific is the largest and deepest, located east of the Philippines.
Most meteorites splash into the ocean because water covers most of Earth's surface!
From space, Earth looks blue — that's why it's called the "blue planet"! Much of its surface is covered with oceans. Other planets look red, brown, or orange because they have no oceans.

How is an island country different from a continent?

The Philippines is surrounded by water with many separate land pieces! Unlike a big connected continent like China, we need a boat or plane to cross islands.
Did you know the ocean is the main source of water vapor? That's because a huge 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water!

Why do we call Earth the "blue planet"?

About three-quarters of Earth's surface is covered by water! That huge amount of water is exactly why our home is called the "blue planet"!
About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water! That is why we call it the Blue Planet.

How much of Earth is actually land?

Only about 29% of Earth's surface is land! The rest of the surface is water.
The ocean covers about 71 percent of Earth's surface, which is way more than the land!
The shore of the Dead Sea is the lowest land on Earth, sitting about 430 meters below sea level!
Wow, about 71 percent of Earth's surface is covered by water!
Earth is the only planet in our solar system with liquid water on its surface and known life!

How much of Earth is actually dry land?

Only about 29 percent of Earth's surface is land—the rest is water!

Where is most of Earth's liquid water hiding?

The world's oceans hold about 97 percent of all the liquid water on Earth's surface!

How big would Earth's water be if gathered into a single sphere?

It would be about 1,385 kilometers wide, which is actually smaller than our Moon!

Where is most of Earth's fresh water stored?

Glaciers and ice caps hold about 68.7 percent of Earth's fresh water, with most of it locked in Antarctica!

How much of Earth's water can we actually drink?

Only 2.5 percent is freshwater, and most of it is frozen in glaciers and ice caps!
Glaciers and ice caps hold about 68 percent of Earth's fresh water, while underground aquifers account for about 30 percent!

How much of Earth's water is salty?

Approximately 97 percent of all water on Earth is salty! You can find this salty water in our five major oceans.

Where is most of Earth's water hiding?

Over 97% of Earth's water is salty! Most of the remaining freshwater is locked away in glaciers.
The Pacific Ocean covers about 32 percent of Earth's surface area, making it larger than all landmasses combined!

Where is most of Earth's fresh water hidden?

Massive glaciers lock up about 69 percent of all the fresh water on planet Earth!
Oceans cover about 71% of Earth's surface and hold roughly 97% of all the water on our entire planet!

briefs.competency: gather information from the Department of Science and Technology (DOST) and other reliable websites to identify how authorities support communities affected by typhoons
briefs.content_standard: Distribution of the continents | Crustal features and interactions | Typhoons | Tides
existing_facts_en:
Who watches out for the habagat, amihan, and storms?

PAGASA! It is the government agency that monitors the weather to warn us about heavy rain or storms.

Why does PAGASA issue storm surge warnings?

To alert coastal communities and keep them safe before a typhoon arrives!
The NDRRMC is the main government agency that coordinates disaster response for floods and typhoons across the Philippines.

Who do you call for help during a typhoon?

Call 911 for emergency assistance! You can also reach the Red Cross or NDRRMC hotline for rescue and relief operations.
After a strong typhoon, towns may need months or years to recover. Rebuilding homes and schools needs government and international help.

The Philippines has agencies watching out for us: PAGASA tracks weather and typhoons, PHIVOLCS monitors earthquakes and volcanoes, MGB watches for landslides, and NDRRMC coordinates disaster response!

briefs.competency: draw on information from secondary sources to identify situations where tidal difference could be exploited to generate renewable energy
briefs.content_standard: Distribution of the continents | Crustal features and interactions | Typhoons | Tides
existing_facts_en: Wave energy is different from tidal energy! It comes from wind-made waves on the sea, and their up-and-down bobbing is turned into electricity.

Why do some wind turbines stand out in the sea?

They stand in the sea because the wind there is stronger and steadier!

Can our local winds make energy?

In the Philippines, the strong amihan and habagat monsoon winds can be a source of wind energy!
The ocean's rise and fall of tides and waves can be turned into electricity! It’s renewable because the ocean keeps moving.
The energy from the rising and falling of ocean tides, called tidal energy, can also be turned into electricity!
Narrow Philippine straits like Sibutu Passage and San Bernardino Strait have tidal energy potential — fast sea currents could drive underwater turbines.
A tidal barrage is a huge wall built across a bay or estuary. As the tide rises and falls, the height difference drives turbines and generators to make predictable electricity!

What causes the cool sea breezes in Batangas?

They are caused by convection! Warm air over land rises up, and cooler sea air moves in to replace it.
During the amihan season, the Philippines experiences cool, dry northeast winds! They bring clear skies and lower temperatures.

briefs.competency: explain that the mechanical energy of an object is the sum of the kinetic energy and the potential energy available to do work
briefs.content_standard: Acceleration | Distance-time and Velocity-time graphs | Kinetic and Potential energy | Work and energy | Renewable energy | Properties of light
existing_facts_en: Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic energy (from motion) and potential energy (from position). Together, they tell us an object's total energy!
Total energy never decreases, but in each transformation it spreads out more evenly. So the energy available for useful work steadily declines!

How do scientists calculate kinetic energy?

The formula is KE = 1/2 x m x v x v! Half the mass times speed squared. Bigger mass or speed means more energy, measured in joules!
Mechanical energy is the total of kinetic energy plus potential energy — without friction, this total stays the same as energy shifts between the two forms!

How do we calculate gravitational potential energy?

It increases with height and mass! We calculate it using GPE = mgh, where m is mass, g is 9.8 m/s², and h is height.
A hand-crank generator uses your muscle power to rotate a magnet inside a coil of wire! It converts mechanical energy into electrical energy that can light an LED!
Mechanical energy is the total sum of an object's kinetic energy and potential energy!
A 100-kilogram roller coaster at the top of a 30-meter hill stores exactly 29,400 joules of gravitational potential energy!

How much energy does a roller coaster store at the top?

A 1,000-kilogram roller coaster car at 50 meters high holds 490,000 joules of potential energy! It all turns into kinetic energy as it zooms down.
The strong winds of a typhoon carry powerful mechanical energy — enough to uproot banana trees!

What energy does a flying Philippine eagle have?

It has kinetic energy from its motion and gravitational potential energy from its altitude!

What kinds of energy does a rolling ball have as it moves down a hill?

It possesses both kinetic energy from its motion and gravitational potential energy from its height!
A 1,000-kilogram car moving at 20 meters per second has four times more kinetic energy than the same car moving at just 10 meters per second!
Water at the top of Angel Falls, the world's highest waterfall at 979 meters, holds massive gravitational potential energy!
A 2-kilogram book held 3 meters above the ground has exactly 58.8 joules of gravitational potential energy!
Eating one medium apple gives you about 95 kilocalories of chemical energy — that's the same mechanical energy needed to lift 40,000 kilograms one meter high!

briefs.competency: gather information from secondary sources to discuss the regular occurrence of meteor showers
briefs.content_standard: Scale, proportion and quantity | Plate boundaries | Structure of the Earth | Geologic time | Origin of the Solar System | Space Technologies
existing_facts_en:
Why do space rocks have three different names?

A meteoroid is in space, a meteor glows in the sky, and a meteorite lands on the ground!

Why do we see so many shooting stars at once during a meteor shower?

Earth passes through a comet's dust trail! Many tiny pieces burn up in the atmosphere at the same time, creating lots of shooting stars in one night.
Meteor showers happen around the same time every year! Earth passes through the same comet dust trail annually, so astronomers know when to expect the Perseids and Geminids.
A shooting star glows because of strong friction with the air! Falling fast through the atmosphere heats it up until it shines.

Why do some meteor showers happen at the exact same time every year?

It's because Earth passes through the same comet-debris path during each orbit!

Where is the best place to spot shooting stars?

On a clear, dark night sky, far away from bright city lights!
A meteor shower happens when Earth passes through the dusty trail left behind by a comet!

Where do shooting stars burn up?

The mesosphere is the third layer and the coldest part of the atmosphere — this is where most meteors burn up before reaching the ground!

Where do meteor showers like the Perseids and Leonids come from?

Meteor showers happen when Earth passes through a comet's debris trail! The Perseids in August come from Comet Swift-Tuttle, and the Leonids in November come from Comet Tempel-Tuttle.
Look up at the sky! The Perseid meteor shower happens every August each year.
Look up in November! The beautiful Leonid meteor shower happens every single year.
A meteor shower happens when Earth passes through a comet's dusty trail! These tiny bits burn up in the atmosphere, creating many streaks of light across the sky.
A shooting star isn't really a star at all! It's actually a small space rock burning up in the atmosphere.
A meteor shower happens when many meteors are seen in the sky on the same night!
A 'shooting star' is not really a star! It's a tiny space rock burning up from friction as it races through Earth's air — making a bright streak of light!

What are shooting stars during the Perseid meteor shower?

They are actually tiny pieces of space dust burning up in Earth's atmosphere, observed by Filipino students and astronomers!
When Earth passes through comet Swift-Tuttle's dusty trail, tiny space particles burn up in our atmosphere and create the Perseid meteor shower!

Why do meteor showers happen at the same time every year?

Earth passes through a trail of dust left by a comet! As the dust particles burn up in the atmosphere each year, we see a meteor shower!

How do meteor showers get their names?

They're named after the constellation they seem to come from! For example, the Perseids come from Perseus, and the Geminids come from Gemini!

briefs.competency: use information from secondary sources to explain the beneficial, harmful, and neutral effects of mutations
briefs.content_standard: DNA replication and mutations | Biodiversity and endangered species | Types of ecosystems in the Philippines
existing_facts_en: Not all mutations are harmful — some are neutral with no effect, some are harmful like those causing cancer, and some are beneficial and help organisms survive.
A mutation can be helpful, harmful, or have no effect at all — most changes to genes don't hurt or help, they're just neutral.

Is a mutation always bad?

No! A mutation is a change in an organism's DNA, and it can be harmless, harmful, or even helpful for survival.
People with just one sickle cell gene get partial protection from malaria — a reason a harmful gene can survive in a population through natural selection.

Why do new virus variants appear?

Viruses can change or mutate over time — that's why new forms or variants sometimes show up.

What is a mutation?

A mutation is a change in DNA — it might do nothing, help, or hurt the living thing that has it!

What is a silent mutation?

Not all mutations show. In a silent mutation, a DNA letter changes but the protein stays the same — like a typo you can still read as the same word.

Can you feel a mutation happening?

No! Cells and DNA are so tiny that you feel nothing at the exact moment a mutation happens — many people carry mutations they never even notice their whole lives.

How can one tiny gene change cause disease?

Genes use DNA to build proteins, the tiny machines that run your body. Change a letter in a gene, and the protein's shape can go wrong — that's how some mutations cause disease.

What makes macapuno coconut so special?

A natural mutation in its seed gives macapuno almost no water and a soft, thick, jelly-like meat instead.

How can a tiny mutation cause cancer?

Cells normally follow rules about when to divide and stop. If mutations build up in the genes controlling this, it's like the brakes breaking — the cell divides out of control. That's cancer.

briefs.competency: identify the number of valence electrons of oxygen based on its position in the periodic table
briefs.content_standard: Valid and reliable investigations | Chemical bonding | Ionic compounds | Covalent compounds | Metallic bonds | Chemical formula

briefs.competency: identify modern scientific processes used to detect and measure the displacement of tectonic plates
briefs.content_standard: Plate Tectonics | Global climate | Global interactions | Global and local Sustainability
existing_facts_en: Scientists use GPS and satellites to track the plates! They measure exactly how fast and in what direction they move.
Many times in Earth's long history, the magnetic north and south poles have swapped places! Scientists know this from minerals frozen in old rocks on the ocean floor.
After a big earthquake, seismographs keep recording aftershocks! These smaller tremors help scientists know if the ground is finally settling down.
Tectonic plates move just a few centimeters per year — about as fast as your fingernail grows! Scientists measure this slow movement using GPS satellites.
A seismograph is an instrument that measures and records ground shaking during an earthquake. It is used by PHIVOLCS here in the Philippines!

Did all the continents used to be connected?

Yes! Millions of years ago, they formed one giant landmass called Pangaea, slowly drifting apart as the tectonic plates moved.
We know seafloor spreading is real because of symmetrical magnetic stripes in the rocks! The sea floor is also youngest near the ridge.
Tectonic plates move super slowly — just a few centimeters per year, about as fast as your fingernails grow! But over millions of years, they move whole continents.

briefs.competency: predict the position and shape of the Philippine Archipelago in 50 million years, based on the current velocity of the Philippine Plate
briefs.content_standard: Plate Tectonics | Global climate | Global interactions | Global and local Sustainability
existing_facts_en: The plates move super slowly — only a few centimeters each year, about as fast as your fingernails grow!

Does the mantle move fast?

No, it flows incredibly slowly! Only a few centimeters per year, about as slow as your fingernails grow, so we never feel it.

How fast do the plates at the Philippine Trench move?

Very slowly! Only a few centimeters a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. But over millions of years, this shapes the sea!
Tectonic plates move super slowly — just a few centimeters per year, about as fast as your fingernails grow! But over millions of years, they move whole continents.
Since plates keep moving, Earth's map today looks totally different from millions of years ago — and the continents will shift again in the coming millions of years!

How fast do Earth's tectonic plates move?

They move about 2 to 15 centimeters per year! That is roughly the exact same speed that your human fingernails grow.

briefs.competency: use models to investigate elastic or inelastic collisions and describe the forces involved and their effects
briefs.content_standard: Projectile motion | Momentum and Collisions | Large-scale generation and distribution of electricity | Renewable and non-renewable energy
existing_facts_en: In a perfectly inelastic collision, objects join together right after they hit, and then they move along as just one single object!
In a Newton's cradle, when one ball hits the row, the momentum travels through the middle balls and the last ball swings out!

What happens when objects crash into each other?

In some crashes, objects bounce apart! In others, they stick together and move as one big lump!

Ever wonder how billiard balls move after a hit?

In a collision, momentum transfers! The moving ball gives its momentum to the resting ball, making it move.
When objects bump, kinetic energy passes between them! In billiards or marbles, a moving ball hits a still one—and suddenly, that still ball zooms away!

What cool toy uses pendulums to show how energy moves?

Newton's cradle! It has hanging balls in a row — release one, and only the far end ball swings out!

briefs.competency: identify and explain that to change the momentum of an object, it is necessary to apply a force on the object over a period of time
briefs.content_standard: Projectile motion | Momentum and Collisions | Large-scale generation and distribution of electricity | Renewable and non-renewable energy
existing_facts_en: Impulse is force multiplied by the time it acts! This is exactly what causes a change in an object's momentum.
Stretch out the time of an impact, and the force you feel gets smaller! Same momentum change, but much safer!
A crumple zone is the part of a car designed to crush and fold in a crash! This makes the impact take longer, lowering the force on passengers.
In a crash, an airbag inflates fast to give your head and chest more time to stop, making the hitting force much smaller!
Force is how quickly an object's momentum changes, so the faster you change its momentum, the larger the force required!

Why is it harder to stop heavy or fast objects?

Because they have greater momentum! This means you need a larger force or a longer time to bring them fully to a stop.
The change in an object's momentum depends on how strong the force is and how long that force acts!
An airbag makes your body stop more slowly during a crash, so the push on you feels much softer and safer!
When a car crashes and stops suddenly, your body keeps its forward momentum! The seatbelt holds you tight, slowly reducing your momentum so you don't hit hard.

How do the thick boxing gloves protect your hands from getting hurt during a punch?

The thick padding in boxing gloves stretches out the time of a punch's impact! This lowers the force at each instant and reduces injury.

Why do baseball players swing and 'follow through' after hitting the ball?

It's not just force strength — it's HOW LONG it acts! A longer contact means a bigger change in motion. Follow-through keeps your bat on the ball longer so it flies farther!

What is impulse, and how does it change momentum?

Impulse equals force multiplied by time! It changes an object's momentum. The longer you apply force, the bigger the change in momentum!
Crumple zones in cars extend collision time! Since impulse equals force times time, a longer collision means less force hits the passengers — keeping them safer!
In an egg drop, soft padding makes the egg stop more slowly. This lessens the impact force so your egg stays safe and does not break!
Wearing a padded helmet protects your head! It absorbs kinetic energy during a fall, reducing the harmful force on your skull.

Why should you bend your knees when landing from a jump?

It increases impact time, reducing the physical force on your leg bones and preventing fractures!

briefs.competency: gather information from secondary sources to identify ways to reduce the impact of collisions such as seatbelts, airbags, and crumple zones in vehicles
briefs.content_standard: Projectile motion | Momentum and Collisions | Large-scale generation and distribution of electricity | Renewable and non-renewable energy
existing_facts_en: Wearing a helmet when biking helps protect your brain if you fall or crash!

How does a steel car protect passengers in a crash?

The strong steel body absorbs and spreads the crash force so it doesn't hit passengers directly! Because steel is tough and doesn't break easily, it keeps people inside safe.

How do bicycle helmets protect your brain?

The crushable foam inside absorbs impact energy during a physical collision to keep your brain safe!
Stretch out the time of an impact, and the force you feel gets smaller! Same momentum change, but much safer!
A crumple zone is the part of a car designed to crush and fold in a crash! This makes the impact take longer, lowering the force on passengers.
In a crash, an airbag inflates fast to give your head and chest more time to stop, making the hitting force much smaller!
A seatbelt holds you in place when a car suddenly stops, keeping you safe from flying forward!
An airbag makes your body stop more slowly during a crash, so the push on you feels much softer and safer!
When a car crashes and stops suddenly, your body keeps its forward momentum! The seatbelt holds you tight, slowly reducing your momentum so you don't hit hard.
Double your speed, and kinetic energy becomes FOUR times bigger—not just double! That's because it depends on speed squared. This is why speeding on roads is super dangerous!

How do the thick boxing gloves protect your hands from getting hurt during a punch?

The thick padding in boxing gloves stretches out the time of a punch's impact! This lowers the force at each instant and reduces injury.
In a crash, your car stops suddenly, but your body wants to keep moving! The seatbelt applies a force to slow you down safely instead of throwing you forward. That's force changing motion!
Crumple zones in cars extend collision time! Since impulse equals force times time, a longer collision means less force hits the passengers — keeping them safer!

Why does a helmet protect your head in a bike crash?

The helmet's soft padding soaks up the crash's force so it doesn't hit your skull directly!

How does a seatbelt keep you safe during a crash?

It stops your body from flying forward because of inertia, keeping you safe and secure!
In an egg drop, soft padding makes the egg stop more slowly. This lessens the impact force so your egg stays safe and does not break!

How do seatbelts keep us safe in a sudden car crash?

Seatbelts protect us by providing an unbalanced force to counteract our forward inertia during a sudden car crash!

Why is it so important to wear a helmet when riding your bike?

A moving bicycle possesses kinetic energy, which is why wearing a helmet protects your head during a crash!

Why wear a helmet when biking?

Gravity accelerates falling objects downward! A helmet protects your head from severe impact injuries during bike crashes.
Wearing a seatbelt applies a stopping force to your forward kinetic energy during a crash, preventing severe impact injuries!
Wearing a padded helmet protects your head! It absorbs kinetic energy during a fall, reducing the harmful force on your skull.
Crash test dummies used by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration demonstrate Newton's first law of inertia by jerking forward during simulated collisions!

briefs.competency: recognize that scientists: a. use chemical equations to describe chemical reactions, and b. write equations in word form and using formula for common chemical reactions
briefs.content_standard: Chemical reactions | Acids, bases, and salts | Types of chemical reactions | Chemical reactions in the environment | Chemical equations | Rates of reactions
existing_facts_en: When wood or gas burns completely, it produces carbon dioxide and water vapor!

How does neutralization actually work?

An acid has extra H+ and a base has extra OH-. When mixed, they join to form water (H2O), so it's no longer strongly acidic or basic!
When an acid meets a base, two things form: a salt and water. The basic recipe is: acid + base = salt + water!

Did you know our table salt comes from neutralization?

When hydrochloric acid mixes with sodium hydroxide (a strong base), the result is table salt and water. Ordinary salt is a product of an acid and a base!

Does a strong acid need a lot of base to neutralize?

Yes, the amount matters! To fully neutralize a strong acid, you need enough base to match all the H+ it releases. If there's not enough base, some acid is left over.
In a chemical equation, reactants are the starting substances before a reaction. Products are the new substances formed after, and they are separated by an arrow!
We balance a chemical equation by adding coefficients! This makes sure the number of each atom is exactly the same on the reactant and product sides.

How do we read a chemical equation?

Reactants go on the left of the arrow, and products on the right! The arrow simply means 'yields' or 'becomes.'

What is the simple recipe for photosynthesis?

It's carbon dioxide + water + sunlight → sugar (glucose) + oxygen! The left side has the ingredients (reactants), and the right side has the products. No atoms disappear, they just rearrange.

briefs.competency: use information from secondary sources to identify examples of modern biotechnology, such as genetically modified organisms and processes (e.g. in vitro fertilization)
briefs.content_standard: Homeostasis | Mechanisms of evolution | Biotechnology | Ecosystem's carrying capacity and population growth
existing_facts_en: Tissue culture grows plants in the lab — a tiny plant piece is placed in special nutrient gel to produce many identical copies.

How do scientists use firefly chemicals?

Scientists put the firefly's glowing chemical, luciferin, into cells to make them light up — so they can see if a medicine is working or if the cells are still alive.
Filipino scientists at centers like IRRI study rice DNA to breed rice that survives drought better or is more nutritious, helping farmers across the country.

What is recombinant DNA?

Recombinant DNA technology lets scientists move a gene from one living thing to another — like putting the human insulin gene into bacteria to make insulin for diabetics.
To make some vaccines, the virus is first grown inside chicken eggs or lab cells, then purified and turned into the vaccine.
The measles vaccine is given as a small shot, usually in the arm or shoulder — a quick little pinch that does a lot to keep you healthy.
To make some vaccines, scientists weaken or kill the germ in a lab until it can't cause disease anymore, using just enough for the body to safely learn to recognize it.

What happens in genetic engineering?

Scientists carefully move a gene from one living thing into another, giving it a new ability — like making a certain protein.
Golden Rice is a GMO rice with extra genes that let it make beta-carotene — which the body turns into vitamin A — to help children who don't get enough.
In selective breeding, people pick the best organisms over many generations. In genetic engineering, scientists change the genes directly — getting the same trait much faster!
Golden Rice is genetically modified to produce beta-carotene, which the human body converts into vitamin A to help prevent blindness.

What does GMO mean?

GMO stands for genetically modified organism — a plant or animal whose genes were changed on purpose to give it a helpful trait.
In tissue culture, plant cells are grown on a sterile nutrient mix with hormones to make many identical plant clones, kept free from bacteria and fungi.

When was the first test-tube baby born?

The world's first test-tube baby, Louise Brown, was born in 1978!
Scientists at IRRI in Los Baños, Laguna, and PhilRice work hard to develop new rice varieties that resist disease and give bigger harvests.

How does Bt corn fight off caterpillars?

Bt corn is a GMO with an added gene from the bacterium Bacillus thuringiensis, making it produce a protein that kills caterpillars that eat it — so less pesticide is needed.

Is there a cure for dengue?

There's a vaccine, but it has limits and isn't for everyone — a doctor's advice is needed. There's still no medicine that kills the virus directly; doctors help the body fight while watching the patient and giving enough fluids.
A vaccine has a dead or weakened piece of a germ that trains the immune system to make memory cells, so the body is ready when the real germ arrives.

How does an mRNA vaccine work?

An mRNA vaccine gives body cells instructions to make one harmless piece of a germ's protein, so the immune system learns to recognize and fight the real germ.
Tiny bacteria like E. coli are science's little workers — scientists grow them fast and reprogram them to make medicines, proteins, and enzymes!
Scientists use certain bacteria to help make medicines, like insulin.
mRNA vaccines, like some COVID-19 vaccines, give your body instructions to make one small piece of a germ so your immune system learns to fight it.

What was the first cloned mammal?

Dolly the sheep! She was the first mammal ever cloned from an adult cell, born in 1996.

Do all vaccines contain a whole germ?

Not this newer kind — it holds no whole germ, just instructions that teach your cells to build one small piece so your defenses learn to recognize it.
IRRI created flood-tolerant rice with a special gene called SUB1 -- it can survive up to 2 weeks fully underwater, a big help for farmers in flood-prone areas.

A bioreactor is a large industrial tank used to grow microorganisms at a huge scale, making products like antibiotics and insulin.
